claims.claim: Sort the cells in your body by size, from red blood cells up, and something odd turns up: each size class weighs roughly the same. (Hook, A4: what a viewer who leaves at second two takes away.)
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML (Hatton et al. 2023, PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120, full text); Fig. 4 image https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/2b19/10523466/ada6f41502f5/pnas.2303077120fig04.jpg
claims.note: Results: 'Such an inverse relation implies that a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class (Fig. 4A)'; significance statement: 'cellular biomass in any given logarithmic cell-size class ... approximately independent of cell size'; 'These data reveal a surprising inverse relation' (so 'something odd' is fair). The binned distribution 'only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells (4 x 10-11 g)', which 'from red blood cells up' respects. 'Roughly' is load-bearing: the paper says 'With the exception of this gap, all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude', i.e. up to ~100x between classes (Fig. 4A, female, log axis: plateau ~1 kg, peaks ~5 kg). A viewer who leaves at second two keeps the paper's own headline claim, with its own hedge; nothing false is left behind. 'Your body': Fig. 3 caption, 'very similar patterns are found for female and child'.

claims.claim: A twenty twenty-three study combined over fifteen hundred earlier studies to estimate the body's cells, type by type, and sorted them by size.
claims.note: Date confirmed: electronic pub 18 Sep 2023, print 26 Sep 2023 (PNAS 120(39)). 'Estimate' confirmed ('we estimate total body counts of ~36 trillion cells'); type by type confirmed ('400 known cell types across 60 tissue systems ... 1,264 cell groups'); sorted by size confirmed (26 octave classes). But the number is of 'published sources', not studies: abstract 'data drawn from >1,500 published sources'; Methods 'compiles cell size and count data from more than 1,500 published sources'. The base is the ICRP reference-man catalogue (a reference report), and the paper reserves 'studies' for a subset ('an average and range of values from multiple published studies'). 'Studies' narrows the paper's word into a claim it does not make (A3). Change to 'combined data from over fifteen hundred published sources' (or 'earlier publications'), and the card to '1,500+ SOURCES' (claim 19).

claims.claim: The smallest cells it sorted are red blood cells.
claims.note: Methods: octave bins 'beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes ... We ignored binning cells smaller than erythrocytes (blood platelets and the smallest haploid gamete cells), to avoid fitting the distribution over relatively large gaps.' Results: 'only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells (4 x 10-11 g)'. 'It sorted' correctly avoids saying red cells are the body's smallest cells.

claims.claim: The biggest are muscle fibres, more than a million times heavier.
claims.note: Abstract: 'from the smallest red blood cells to the largest muscle fibers'; Results: 'from a tiny red blood cell to a myocyte, more than a million-fold larger'; the count relation extends 'from red blood cells to the largest myocytes'. The paper's size measure is cell mass in grams (Fig. 3/4 axes 'Cell mass (g)'), so 'heavier' is the same claim. Recomputed: 26 doubling classes from 4e-11 g reach 4e-11 x 2^26 = 2.7e-3 g, ~67 million-fold; the myocyte biomass peak near 1e-4 g is 2.5 million-fold. 'More than a million' is a floor both support.

claims.claim: Now put every cell into a size class, each class twice as heavy as the one before.
claims.note: Doubling confirmed: 'bins increase by a multiplicative factor of 2 from small to large (octave size classes) ... giving 26 size classes'. But 'every cell' is wrong as spoken: the paper explicitly did not bin platelets or the smallest haploid gametes ('We ignored binning cells smaller than erythrocytes'), and the line just before says only that the smallest cells sorted are red blood cells. A viewer hears 'every cell in your body'. Change to 'Now put those cells into size classes, ...' or 'Now put every cell from red blood cells up into a size class, ...'.

claims.claim: Each time the size doubles, there are, on average, about half as many cells.
claims.note: Fig. 3 caption: 'The total number of cells in each of 26 logarithmic size classes is regressed against cell mass (g), giving a slope near -0.97'; Methods: 95% CI -1.09 to -0.87. The regression is count per octave class vs. class size, so per doubling the count changes by 2^-0.97 = 0.51 (CI 0.47-0.55): 'about half'. Results: 'an increase in size by a given factor is offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor'. 'On average' is needed and present: in Fig. 3 individual classes sit off the line (the classes near 1e-5 g fall about an order of magnitude below it).

claims.claim: So the small cells win on numbers, the big cells win on size, and the two cancel out.
claims.note: Paper: 'an increase in size by a given factor is offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor (and vice versa). Such an inverse relation implies that a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class'; abstract speaks of 'a whole-organism trade-off between cell size and count'. 'Cancel out' is the paper's 'offset', approximate, and the next line says 'roughly'. Counts are dominated by small cells ('Cell counts are completely dominated by red blood cells, platelets, and tissue resident white blood cells').

claims.claim: Every class ends up holding roughly the same weight.
claims.note: As claim 1: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class'; 'the cellular biomass is overall approximately evenly spread among cell-size classes (Fig. 4A)'. Qualified at once by the next line's exception, as the paper does.

claims.claim: With one exception: a dip, between the fat cells and the muscle fibres.
claims.note: 'There are also prominent biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10-6 g) and myocytes (near 10-4 g), separated by a gap of relatively low biomass ... With the exception of this gap, all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude.' 'One exception' is the paper's own framing. Caveat seen in Fig. 4 (not in the text): the very last class (largest muscle fibres, ~2e-3 g) also tails off; in the male it stays near the plateau (~0.25 kg vs ~1 kg, Fig. 4B), but in the female and child it is as low as the dip (see claim 37). Acceptable for the spoken line, which is about the body in general and quotes the paper's summary; it does matter for the three-row visual.

claims.claim: In women the dip is smaller, and in a ten-year-old it is fainter still.
claims.note: 'This gap is also evident but less prominent in the reference female, and is even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child (Fig. 4B and SI Appendix, Fig. S5).' Reference child is 10 years old, 32 kg. Fig. 4B agrees: the muscle peak either side of the gap falls from ~7 kg (male) to ~4.5 kg (female) to ~3 kg (child) while the gap floor stays near zero, so the dip is less pronounced in each.

claims.claim: Take a typical man. His muscle fibres are fewer than one in fifty thousand of his cells with a nucleus.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption (reference male): 'Cell biomass is dominated by skeletal myocytes ... even though they make up <0.002% of the nucleated cell count'. 0.002% = 2e-5 = 1 in 50,000; '<' kept as 'fewer than'. Muscle fibre = skeletal myocyte (abstract: 'largest muscle fibers'). 'Typical man' = the paper's 'representative male (70 kg)' / reference male built on the ICRP reference anatomy: fair as 'typical'. Nucleated cell count ~7 trillion (same caption).

claims.claim: Yet they make up about half the weight of all his cells.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: 'Cell biomass is dominated by skeletal myocytes, comprising about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass in the body'; 'the remaining 23.5 kg' implies skeletal myocytes ~21.5 kg (48%). Discussion: myocytes 'make up about half of all cell biomass'.

claims.claim: And all his cells together weigh about forty-five kilograms.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: 'all 45 kg of cell biomass in the body' (reference male).

claims.claim: The other twenty-five of his seventy are not cells at all. They are the water, protein and minerals between them.
claims.note: Fig. 2 caption: 'Cell biomass excludes noncellular components of biomass in each tissue, made up of extracellular water, protein, and minerals (~25 kg; see SI Appendix).' Reference male 70 kg (abstract). 45 + 25 = 70. 'Between them' = extracellular, the paper's word. SI Appendix itself not opened; the main-text figure is what the line states.

claims.claim: Sort the life in the ocean by size, as it was before industrial fishing, and most size classes held about the same weight too.
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8580314/fullTextXML (Hatton et al. 2021, Sci. Adv. 7(46) eabh3732, doi:10.1126/sciadv.abh3732, full text); Fig. 2 image https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/a00d/8580314/ac12b83f0aa6/sciadv.abh3732-f2.jpg
claims.note: Abstract: 'biomass within most order of magnitude size classes is indeed remarkably constant, near 1 gigatonne (Gt) wet weight (10^15 g), but bacteria and large marine mammals are markedly above and below this value, respectively.' The baseline is 'a "pristine" state, before industrial-scale human capture of fish and marine mammals (pre-1850)'. 'Most' and the past tense are both needed and present. The PNAS paper cites it as the same kind of distribution ('bodies in the ocean from bacteria to whales'). The pristine spectrum is a reconstruction from models and historical data, which 'held' slightly firms up, but the paper itself writes 'We find that ...'.

claims.claim: And in your body, nobody knows why. No accepted process explains it yet.
claims.note: Discussion: 'To our knowledge, there is no universally recognized process that accounts for these patterns. Nonetheless, many simple random growth processes are capable of giving a stable inverse size distribution', then candidate mechanisms and 'the actual process is likely a great deal more complex'. 'No accepted process explains it yet' matches; 'nobody knows why' is the plain-English form of 'no universally recognized process' and does not deny that hypotheses exist. Kept confirmed only because the second sentence states the paper's exact limit right after.

claims.claim: Trillions of tiny cells, far fewer giant ones, and roughly the same weight at every size.
claims.note: '≈36 trillion cells in the male', of which non-nucleated blood cells ≈29 trillion; skeletal myocytes <0.002% of the ~7 trillion nucleated cells. 'Roughly the same weight at every size' restates the paper's 'cellular biomass in any given logarithmic cell-size class ... approximately independent of cell size', with the dip already stated in claim 9.

claims.claim: ROUGHLY THE SAME (first and last keyword cards); ABOUT THE SAME
claims.where: on-screen: keyword cards for claims 1, 8 and 17
claims.note: As claims 1, 8 and 17: the paper's 'roughly similar fraction' and 'approximately evenly spread'. The cards keep the hedge.

claims.claim: 1,500+ STUDIES
claims.note: Number confirmed ('>1,500 published sources'), noun not: see claim 2. Change to '1,500+ SOURCES'.

claims.claim: RED BLOOD CELLS (keyword card); axis mark 'RED BLOOD CELLS / FROM 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g'
claims.where: on-screen: claim 3 card and size chart
claims.note: 'only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells (4 x 10-11 g)'; Methods: bins begin 'at the lower bound of erythrocytes'. 'FROM' correctly marks 4e-11 g as the lower bound, not a typical red-cell mass.
As claim 4: 'more than a million-fold larger', size measured as mass.

claims.claim: ×2 EACH CLASS; 26 size classes, each twice the mass of the last, starting at 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g
claims.where: on-screen: claim 5 card and size chart
claims.note: Methods: 'bins increase by a multiplicative factor of 2 ... beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'; Fig. 3 caption '26 logarithmic size classes'. Top edge 4e-11 x 2^26 = 2.7e-3 g, inside the chart's 1e-2 g axis end; Fig. 3/4 bins also end near 2-3e-3 g.

claims.claim: HALF AS MANY
claims.note: 2^-0.97 = 0.51 per doubling (claim 6). The card drops 'on average', but it is shown over that spoken line.

claims.claim: THEY CANCEL OUT
claims.note: As claim 7: the paper's size increase 'offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor'.

claims.claim: ONE DIP
claims.note: As claim 9: 'With the exception of this gap'. One gap is named in the paper.

claims.claim: SMALLER IN WOMEN
claims.note: 'less prominent in the reference female' (claim 10).

claims.claim: A TYPICAL MAN, sub '70 KG (154 LB)'
claims.note: 'representative male (70 kg)'. 70 kg x 2.20462 = 154.3 lb, so 154 LB is correct.

claims.claim: < 1 IN 50,000; dot grid of 250 × 200 dots captioned '50,000 CELLS WITH A NUCLEUS · FEWER THAN 1 MUSCLE FIBRE', one dot ringed
claims.where: on-screen: claim 11 card and dot grid
claims.note: '<0.002% of the nucleated cell count' = fewer than 1 in 50,000. 250 x 200 = 50,000, correct. The single ringed dot could read as 'exactly one'; the caption 'FEWER THAN 1' carries the limit, so it stands. Optional: label the ringed dot 'AT MOST 1'.

claims.claim: ABOUT HALF; bar 'ALL HIS CELLS · 45 KG' half filled, labelled 'MUSCLE FIBRES ≈ HALF'
claims.where: on-screen: claim 12 card and cell-mass bar
claims.note: 'skeletal myocytes, comprising about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass' (~21.5 kg, 48%, from 'the remaining 23.5 kg'). Half filled is accurate to the drawing.

claims.claim: 45 KG, sub '99 LB'
claims.note: 45 kg of cell biomass; 45 x 2.20462 = 99.2 lb, so 99 LB is correct.

claims.claim: NOT CELLS, sub '25 KG (55 LB)'; BETWEEN THE CELLS; bar extends with 'NOT CELLS · 25 KG', '70 KG MAN', 'WATER · PROTEIN · MINERALS', lengths 45:25
claims.where: on-screen: claim 14 cards and extended bar
claims.note: 'noncellular components ... extracellular water, protein, and minerals (~25 kg)'; 70 kg reference male; 45 + 25 = 70, drawn in proportion. 25 x 2.20462 = 55.1 lb, so 55 LB is correct.

claims.claim: THE OCEAN TOO
claims.note: As claim 15; the spoken 'most' and 'before industrial fishing' accompany it, and the ocean chart's title carries the period.

claims.claim: NOBODY KNOWS WHY; NOT YET EXPLAINED
claims.note: As claim 16: 'no universally recognized process that accounts for these patterns'. 'NOT YET EXPLAINED' is the closer of the two; together they hold.

claims.claim: Axis 'CELL MASS IN GRAMS · LOG SCALE' from 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻² g, marks 'FAT CELLS / ~10⁻⁶ g' and 'MUSCLE FIBRES / ~10⁻⁴ g'
claims.note: Paper's size measure is cell mass (g) on log axes (Fig. 3, 4). 'prominent biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10-6 g) and myocytes (near 10-4 g)'. The marks give where those cells' biomass sits, which '~' covers; adipocytes and myocytes have 'uncommonly broad size distributions'. Range 4e-11 to 2.7e-3 g fits inside 1e-11 to 1e-2.

claims.claim: Bars 'NUMBER OF CELLS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC': a straight falling staircase
claims.where: on-screen: count bars on size chart
claims.note: Draws the fitted trend (slope -0.97, near -1) the narration calls 'on average', and says SCHEMATIC (A6). The real class counts scatter about the line, most visibly a drop of about an order of magnitude near 1e-5 g (the same gap as the weight dip). A perfectly straight staircase is the fit, not the data, and the label says so. Optional: a slight notch near 1e-5 g would match the dip shown next.

claims.claim: Bars 'WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC': roughly level, with a dip between the fat and muscle marks
claims.where: on-screen: weight bars on size chart
claims.note: Matches the paper's summary ('approximately evenly spread', 'little systematic variation with log cell mass', gap between adipocyte and myocyte peaks near 1e-5 g, 'With the exception of this gap, all variation ... within two orders of magnitude'). Read off Fig. 4 for the male (the script's 'typical man'): non-gap classes ~0.25-7 kg (within ~1.5 decades, 'roughly level' on a log axis), gap floor ~0.05 kg. Two simplifications, both covered by SCHEMATIC: the fat and muscle peaks either side of the dip (~5x the plateau) are flattened, and the last class tails off. Optional: small bumps either side of the dip.

claims.claim: Three stacked rows of level bars 'MAN', 'WOMAN', 'CHILD, 10', titled 'WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC', dip shallower in each row down
claims.note: The dip ordering is right ('less prominent in the reference female ... even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child'), and 'CHILD, 10' matches the 10-year-old reference child. But the rows draw every other class level, and Fig. 4 contradicts that at the top end for WOMAN and CHILD: their last class (largest muscle fibres, ~2e-3 g) falls to about the level of the dip, near zero in Fig. 4B and ~20 g against a ~1 kg plateau and a ~50 g dip on Fig. 4A's female log axis. A row showing one shallow dip and a level end therefore shows a woman's and child's distribution flatter than the paper's figure. Change: let the final bar drop in the WOMAN and CHILD rows (to about dip depth) and slightly in the MAN row (~0.25 kg vs ~1 kg), or end all three rows before the last class. SCHEMATIC covers the scale, not a shape the data contradicts.

claims.claim: Ocean card: axis 'SIZE OF SEA LIFE, BACTERIA TO WHALES · LOG SCALE', level bars titled 'BEFORE INDUSTRIAL FISHING · SCHEMATIC', first two bars higher and last two lower
claims.note: Axis wording matches the paper's title, 'The global ocean size spectrum from bacteria to whales'; pre-1850 'pristine' baseline. Fig. 2 caption: 'Total estimated historic ocean biomass in each order of magnitude size class is approximately 1 Gt ..., with exceptions at either extreme.' Fig. 2A (upper 200 m, log): the first two tenfold classes (10^-14 to 10^-12 g, bacteria and picophytoplankton) ~2.4 Gt, the third ~1.9 Gt, most others ~0.6-1 Gt; the last two (mammal-dominated) ~0.12 and ~0.06 Gt, the one before ~0.46 Gt. So 'first two higher, last two lower' is right in direction and the clearest cases; the third class at each end is milder. Within SCHEMATIC. Optional: make the third bar at each end slightly off-level. The full-depth mesopelagic hump (0.01-1 g) is left out, as the paper 'hesitate[s] to draw a strong conclusion' about it.
